doc.title: Orrin Evans interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 22, 2018

chapter: The barber shop and Uncle's saxophone
title: The barber shop as a place of learning
summary: As the youngest he sat in the barber shop for hours, swept hair, ran for food, and learned to take a little from everyone.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Oh man that’s very interesting. Tell me about the — I want to follow-up on something from your website and you talked about the “barber shop” in the African-American community. And I’ve heard just a little bit about that, but can you expand on that at all?

I mean that was, for me that was the place where I learned most things. You know, the time I would go to the barber shop, and for us, since I was the young one, I was the youngest, my brother would drop me off at the barber shop and if there were ten people in front of me and then he would come back, but he might, you know, he’d come back a little later. So I could honestly be in the barber shop for two to three hours on a Saturday just sitting there listening to the conversation. Or they would put on a movie and talk about the movie. So one of my first jobs, that was what I did. I swept hair in the barber shop. And I learned so much you know. Six barbers in there, all different ages, not all men — there were men and women — barbers not, women barbers also in there. And they were different religions, different musical and food taste. There was so much food I tasted for the first time at the barber shop because I would run and get food for people. So one barber wanted it just — I had never had chicken gizzards at that time. And he ordered chicken gizzards all the time. So I would run and get those you know. Or this one wants a sandwich this way. It was life. But it also, for me, how it helped me, I learned how there were so many different people in the barber shop, but then there were also people who didn’t — they were in their little stations. You know like I said, this one only had chicken gizzards every Saturday. This one took a sandwich the same way every week. This one would always sweep his own hair, so I would never have anything to do because he

would sweep, he was like a neat freak. So what I learned, I was like I want to be a combination of everyone I meet. I want to grab little things from everybody. But I don’t want to be so particular, you know, that I can’t do this if it’s not this way. And I learned sitting in the barber shop, I did see a lot of that. All the arguments were people were just stuck on their way. So you know, as far as learning from each person it was amazing but I also learned how to open myself up based on the closeness I saw in each station if that makes sense.
